title: Bound 4 Da Reload (Casualty)
label: East West
format: White-label vinyl first (about 1,000 copies, per Oxide in the Guardian interview); commercial CD single on East West (two parts) per Wikipedia
release_date: 2000 (white label earlier; UK chart entry 6 May 2000)
tracklist_note: Wikipedia CD Part 1: Radio Edit / 'Express Da Funk' / 'Bound 4 Da Reload'; Part 2: original, Remix, Video (enhanced CD). Also on the album Execute (charted 9 Jun 2001).

sound_descriptions.text: Built around a sample of the BBC Casualty theme plus a spoken skit from the Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels soundtrack; Neutrino voiced it in one take over Oxide's beat (Guardian 'How we made' interview, c. 2019).

Tom Ewing (Popular, 2015) hears a sparse, skeletal beat with deep, hollow bass, time-stretched samples and gunshot effects; the film clip sits where a chorus would be, and the structure feels fragmented rather than built up.
Ewing describes Neutrino's rough, congested delivery as true to pirate-radio MCing: prepared bars, scatting, call-and-response and simply riding the beat (Popular, 2015).
Wikipedia's infobox labels it 2-step garage; many radio stations reportedly refused to play it because of the spoken sample.

context.text: Entered the Official Singles Chart at no. 1 on 6 May 2000 (15 weeks).
Began as a dubplate for a pirate radio show; the pair met at the pirate station Supreme FM and were members of So Solid Crew before signing as a duo (Guardian interview).

Dan Hancox (RBMA Daily, 2019) names it, with 'I Don't Smoke', as the straws that broke the camel's back in the 'garage wars' between the UKG old guard and MC-led crews; Timmi Magic dismissed it as 'kiddie stuff, going backwards'.
In the Guardian retrospective Neutrino says the track 'sounds like the start of what was becoming grime'.

relationships.other: So Solid Crew – Oh No (Sentimental Things) / Dilemma (CD single carries an 'Oxide Remix')
Oxide & Neutrino – Rap Dis / Only Wanna Know U Cos Ure Famous (2001)

uncertainty: Exact commercial release day not found (Wikipedia: May 2000; chart entry 6 May 2000). No catalogue number seen. The Guardian piece was read through an inkl copy with no date shown; an MN2S post about it is dated 29 Jan 2019, so c. 2019 is inferred. No contemporary (2000) source calling it grime was found; the grime link is retrospective and comes from the artist himself.

title: Oh No (Sentimental Things) / Dilemma
label: Relentless
format: CD single (earliest format verified); other formats not verified
release_date: 2000 (charted on an OCC Hip Hop & R&B chart from 16 Dec 2000)
tracklist_note: CD single: Radio Edit / Full Length Version / Oxide Remix / Dilemma (RareVinyl listing). An 'Oh No' remix is track 3 on the album They Don't Know; 'Dilemma' is not on the album.

sound_descriptions.text: Steve Goodman (Kode9), writing in Deuce in 2001, calls 'Dilemma' 'ultra-minimal'.
The Quietus (2020): 'Dilemma' is a bare-bones rush of spartan drum hits and a mutating bassline, a moody precursor to minimal grime.
The Quietus (2020): 'Oh No' is sharp-angled, with rumbling bass and MC braggadocio, over a beat sitting between Timbaland-style R&B and UK garage two-step; Lisa Maffia sings the chorus.
FACT (2013) calls 'Dilemma' the 'freakishly minimalist proto-grime flip'.

context.text: So Solid Crew are from Battersea, south London, and made their name on the pirate station Delight FM ('So Solid Sundays'), having also been on Supreme FM.
The Quietus (2020) reports that Wiley later called 'Oh No' the record that started grime.
Megaman (Complex, 2021) places the turning point towards grime at 'Oh No (Sentimental Things)', not '21 Seconds', and says the crew still called their music garage at the time.
OCC lists 'Oh No (Sentimental Things)' on its Hip Hop & R&B chart from 16 Dec 2000 (peak 6, 9 weeks); it did not enter the main singles chart.

relationships.other: Musical Mob (Youngstar) – Pulse X (2002)
So Solid Crew – They Don't Know (album, 2001), track 3 'Oh No (Sentimental Things) (Remix)'
Oxide (of Oxide & Neutrino) – 'Oxide Remix' on the CD single

uncertainty: Producer not found. The exact release date and any earlier 12-inch or white-label issue were not verified. RareVinyl lists 'Oh No' as the lead title, while the Quietus calls 'Oh No' the B-side to 'Dilemma' and FACT calls 'Dilemma' the 'flip', so which side was the A-side is unclear. OCC's chart placement on a Hip Hop & R&B *albums* chart looks odd and may be a data quirk. Wiley's attribution is reported second-hand by the Quietus.

title: 21 Seconds
label: Relentless
tracklist_note: Second single from They Don't Know (album track 17). Opens with a clip of Lisa Maffia's young daughter. Megaman says the label asked for a chorus and more length, so the single runs about five minutes.

sound_descriptions.text: Wikipedia: fairly stripped-back 2-step garage at about 140 BPM in G minor; each MC gets a short slot (the title's 21 seconds).
Complex (2021) describes synthesised keys, skeletal drums and a barrage of garage MCs; Megaman says everyone did 8 bars each.
The Quietus (2020) has ten MCs each taking a turn over a 'rinkadink garage backing'.

context.text: Official Singles Chart no. 1 (first chart date 18 Aug 2001, 18 weeks) and Dance chart no. 1. It also appears on the Independent Singles chart from 19 May 2001, earlier than the commercial release.
Complex (2021) says the track helped usher in the sound and scene 'that later became known as grime'.
The Quietus (2020) calls it a blueprint for crew grime records such as More Fire Crew's 'Pow!'.
Vice (2017) places So Solid in the gap between UK garage's peak and grime's birth, arguing 'they did it first'.

relationships.other: Lethal Bizzle – Pow! (Forward) (2004) [the Quietus says More Fire Crew's 'Pow!']
So Solid Crew – They Don't Know (album, 2001)

uncertainty: Bar counts conflict: Megaman says 8 bars each, while Wikipedia's text says 12 bars of 4 beats. The 19 May 2001 Independent chart entry suggests an earlier independent or white-label issue that was not verified. Complex names no producer; the Synth credit comes from Wikipedia only.

title: They Don't Know
label: Independiente / Relentless
tracklist_note: 20 tracks, including 'Haters', 'Oh No (Sentimental Things) (Remix)', 'They Don't Know', 'Deeper', 'In My Life', 'Ride wid Us' and '21 Seconds'.

sound_descriptions.text: The Quietus (2020) hears a maximal record of sub bass, distorted synth lines and serrated drum hits, with drums drawing on dancehall, 2-step, house and hip hop.
The Quietus singles out 'Deeper' (two-step beat, bass thump; 'grime avant la lettre') and 'In My Life' (metallic bass recalling early dubstep).
Vice (2017) describes 'a raw and forward-facing futurism' and calls the title track a blend of ragga, garage beats, clipped delivery and R&B.

context.text: Official Albums Chart peak no. 6 (first chart date 1 Dec 2001, 23 weeks). The title-track single reached no. 3 (17 Nov 2001) and no. 1 on the Dance chart.
Certified Platinum by the BPI, per Wikipedia.
Vice (2017) frames So Solid as active before grime had a formal identity, in the gap between UKG's peak and grime's birth.

title: Know We
label: Solid City (per Reynolds); FACT calls it self-released; RBMA says Wiley later signed it to Teebone
format: Dubplate from late 1999, then vinyl (white labels sold to shops by Wiley, per RBMA)
tracklist_note: Debut single of the crew. Per RBMA, Wiley later licensed it to Teebone in a bundle with 'Terrible' and 'Wickedest Ting'.

sound_descriptions.text: Reynolds (Wire 'Grime Primer', 2005, reposted 2015): simple programmed beats and a single violin-flourish hook, with the MCs carrying the track.
Trench (2019): ominous string riffs and harder-hitting drum sequences, like 'a rap cypher in a rave'.
FACT (2013): gritty and gruff, with a skeletal rhythm and bass drone and the MC as the focus.
Mixmag (2018): 'clearly demarcated space for MCs to fill with complex rhymes'.

context.text: A dubplate circulated from late 1999 before the official 2000 release; the crew grew out of shows on the pirate station Rinse FM (Wikipedia).
Reynolds (2005) says it was on dubplate from 1999 and in constant pirate rotation before release; Trench (2019) notes that members Geeneus and Slimzee co-founded Rinse FM.
Crew members included Wiley, Maxwell D, Flowdan, God's Gift, Slimzee, DJ Target, Geeneus, Breeze, Plague, Bubbles and Major Ace; remnants later formed Roll Deep.
Mixmag's Dan Hancox (2018) claims it as the first grime track: a paradigm shift from dark garage to MC-centred tracks.
RBMA (2015): 'Know We' started a buzz for the Pay As U Go and Bow crews, with Wiley selling white labels directly to shops.

relationships.other: Roll Deep Entourage – Terrible (Reynolds calls them a chip-off-the-same-block pair; shops treated Terrible as its follow-up)
Pay As U Go – Champagne Dance (2002)

uncertainty: Year conflicts: 2000 (Wikipedia, FACT, Mixmag) vs 2001 (Reynolds). Label conflicts: Solid City (Reynolds), self-released (FACT), later Teebone (RBMA). No catalogue number found because Discogs was unavailable. Reynolds's 2001 'Unfaves of 2000' text reposted in the same post describes the 2001 pirate garage-rap sound generally, so it was not assigned to this record specifically.

Trench (2022) says it spread mostly via pirate radio, local shops and raves; by 2002 the crew had a 1Xtra Sunday show.
